The Fatal Guarantee
The Escape Plan: Escudero and his brothers plan to
flee Acapulco on horseback to join armed peasant
supporters in the mountains.
The Mother's Plea: Doña Irene, terrified for her sons,
negotiates with the military via a local priest. The military
promises them safety if they surrender. She threatens to
throw herself in a well if they ride away.
The Surrender: Knowing the promises are lies
(*Where are the guarantees they offered you?"),
Escudero yields to his mother.
The Capture: Soldiers break down the door. Juan,
Francisco, and Felipe are locked inside Fort San Diego
while the merchants finalize the assassination payment.

December 20, 1923: Aguacatillo
12:00 AM: The brothers are driven out of town
in a truck owned by a Gachupin soap factory.
1:00 AM: Stood against
a wall in the dark.
Felipe (22 years old):
14 rifle shots.
Francisco (30 years old):
7 rifle shots.
Juan R. (33 years old): Shot by the squad, then
approached by Captain Morlett who places
a pistol to the bridge of his nose and fires the
second tiro de gracia of Escudero's life.

The Final Miracle
Dawn: A peasant finds the bodies.
Incredibly, the tiro de gracia deflected
off Juan's skull. He is alive.
The Procession: Rumors spread.
A massive crowd of men and women
abandon Acapulco and march out to
the execution site. The merchants
are terrified he will resurrect again.
"Sigan adelante, que nuestra
muerte no hava sido en vano."
7:00 PM: Eighteen hours after his
execution, the man who died twice
finally expires in the arms of his
supporters on the dirt road back
to Acapulco.

The Permanent Myth of the Coast
Synthesis Statement
[ The Gachupín monopoly believed that destroying Escudero's body would destroy his movement.
Instead, by forcing a paralyzed man to speak through the youth, and ultimately shooting him
twice to keep him down, they transformed a local mayor into an immortal myth.
The Legacy
Escudero did not just fight a political campaign; he broke the psychological isolation of
Acapulco. He proved that the entrenched power of the Spanish oligarchy could be forced to
answer to a five-centavo newspaper and a man who danced barefoot in the dirt.
